en: The Shorter Exposition:
The Exposition of the Chapter on the Way to the Far Shore;
The Exposition of the Questions.
15. The Exposition of the Young Brahmin Mogharāja’s Question “I shall ask Sakka,” [said the Venerable Mogharāja].
The One with Vision did not answer me;
O Queen, I have heard that he answered me only upon the third request.
“Twice, Sakka, that brahmin asked a question of the Buddha, the Blessed One.
When the Blessed One was asked the question, he did not answer it, [thinking]:
‘In the interval between these two times, this brahmin’s faculties will reach maturity.’”
He is a Sakka because he is capable (*sakkoti*).
Alternatively, he is a Sakka because the Blessed One went forth from the Sakya clan (*sakya-kula*).
Or else, he is a Sakka because he is wealthy, possessing great riches and wealth.
For him, these are the riches, namely: the riches of faith,
the riches of virtue, the riches of moral shame, the riches of moral dread, the riches of learning, the riches of generosity, the riches of wisdom, the riches of the foundations of mindfulness,
the riches of the right efforts, the riches of the bases of psychic power, the riches of the faculties, the riches of the powers, and the riches of the factors of enlightenment.
The wealth of the path, the wealth of the fruit, and the wealth of Nibbāna.
Because he is enriched by these many kinds of wealth and treasures, Sakka is called "the wealthy one" (*dhanavā*) and "one of great wealth" (*mahaddhana*).

Alternatively, Sakka is so called because he is powerful (*pahu*), capable (*visavī*), self-sufficient (*alamatto*), brave (*sūra*), heroic (*vīra*), valiant (*vikkanta*), fearless (*abhīrū*), undaunted (*acchambhī*), unafraid (*anutrāsī*), not fleeing (*apalāyī*), having abandoned fear and terror (*pahīnabhayabherava*), and being free from horripilation (*vigatalomahaṃsa*). Thus he is Sakka.
"Twice I shall question Sakka; twice I shall question Sakka, I shall entreat him, I shall beseech him, I shall inspire confidence in him—twice I shall question Sakka.
Thus spoke the Venerable Mogharāja.
“Iccā” is a phonetic conjunction; “...pe...”;
“āyasmā” is a term of endearment; “...pe...”;
“Mogharāja” is the name of that brahmin; “...pe...”; “abhilāpo” means speech.
Thus spoke the Venerable Mogharāja:
"He did not explain the eye to me.

"He did not explain to me" means he did not explain it, did not point it out, did not teach it, did not define it, did not establish it, did not uncover it, did not analyze it, did not make it clear, and did not reveal it.
The Blessed One is possessed of vision through five kinds of vision:

he is possessed of vision through the fleshly eye, he is possessed of vision through the divine eye, he is possessed of vision through the wisdom-eye, he is possessed of vision through the Buddha-eye, and he is possessed of vision through the universal eye.
How is the Blessed One possessed of vision through the fleshly eye?
In the Blessed One’s fleshly eye, five colors are found:
the blue color, the yellow color, the red color, the black color, and the white color.
And where the eyelashes are set, that is blue—deep blue, serene, beautiful, and like the flax flower.
Beyond that, his eyebrows are yellowish, beautifully yellow, golden-hued, inspiring, lovely to behold, and like *kaṇikāra* flowers.
Both of the Blessed One’s eye-sockets are red, beautifully red, inspiring, lovely to behold, and like *indagopaka* insects.
In the middle, they are black, beautifully black, not coarse, glossy, inspiring, lovely to behold, and like *addāriṭṭhaka* seeds.
Beyond that, it becomes white, very white, bright, pure, pleasing, beautiful, and like the morning star.
With that ordinary fleshly eye, comprised within his own physical form and produced by past deeds of wholesome conduct, the Blessed One sees for a league all around, both by day and by night.
This is when there is darkness endowed with four factors and the sun has set.
It was the dark fortnight, the Uposatha day; there was a dense forest thicket, and a great black cloud had arisen.
In such darkness, endowed with these four factors, he could see for a league all around.
There was no wall, nor door-panel, nor rampart, nor mountain, nor bush, nor creeper that was an obstruction to his seeing forms.
If one were to take a single sesame seed as a sign and drop it into a cartload of sesame seeds, one could pick out that very same sesame seed.
So pure is the Blessed One’s natural flesh-eye.
Thus, the Blessed One is possessed of vision even by means of the flesh-eye.
In what way is the Blessed One possessed of vision through the divine eye?
With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, the Blessed One sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate;
he understands how beings fare according to their kamma.
“Indeed, these worthy beings were possessed of misconduct in body, possessed of misconduct in speech, and possessed of misconduct in mind;
they were revilers of the noble ones, held wrong views, and undertook actions based on wrong views.
With the breakup of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
"Or else, these worthy beings were endowed with good conduct of body, endowed with good conduct of speech, and endowed with good conduct of mind;
they did not revile the noble ones, held right view, and undertook actions based on right view;
at the breaking up of the body, after death, they have reappeared in a happy destination, a heavenly world."
Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn— low and high, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—
and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma. And if the Blessed One so desired, he could see one world-system, he could see two world-systems,
he could see three world-systems, he could see four world-systems, and he could see five world-systems.
He might see ten world-systems; he might see twenty world-systems; he might see thirty world-systems;
he might see forty world-systems; he might see fifty world-systems; he might see a hundred world-systems;
he might see a small thousandfold world-system; he might see a medium two-thousandfold world-system.
He would see a thousandfold world system; he would see a second thousandfold world system; he would see a third thousandfold world system;
or indeed, as far as he might wish, so far would he see.
Thus pure is the Blessed One’s divine eye.
Thus the Blessed One is possessed of vision through the divine eye.
How is the Blessed One possessed of vision through the eye of wisdom?
The Blessed One possesses great wisdom, broad wisdom, swift wisdom, smiling wisdom, sharp wisdom, penetrative wisdom, and is skilled in the analysis of wisdom.

One whose knowledge is fully blossomed, who has attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), who has reached the four grounds of self-confidence, who possesses the ten powers, the bull among men, the lion among men, the elephant among men, the thoroughbred among men, the steed among men;
one of infinite knowledge, infinite majesty, and infinite fame; wealthy, possessing great riches and treasures;
a leader, a guide, an inspirer, one who makes things known, one who causes others to contemplate, one who causes others to look on, and one who inspires confidence.
For the Blessed One is the arouser of the unarisen path, the producer of the unproduced path, the declarer of the undeclared path;
he is the knower of the path, the discoverer of the path, the one skilled in the path; and his disciples now dwell following that path, having subsequently attained it.

For the Blessed One knows what should be known and sees what should be seen; he is become vision, become knowledge, become Dhamma, become Brahma. He is the speaker, the proclaimer, the guide to the goal, the giver of the Deathless, the Lord of the Dhamma, the Tathāgata.
There is nothing unknown, unseen, unperceived, unrealized, or untouched by his wisdom for that Blessed One.
With respect to the past, the future, and the present, all phenomena in every aspect come within the range of the Buddha, the Blessed One’s, gateway of knowledge.
Whatever is called "guidable" (neyya) that there may be to be known—whether for one’s own benefit, for the benefit of others, or for the benefit of both;

whether a benefit pertaining to the present life or a benefit pertaining to future lives; whether a benefit that is shallow or a benefit that is profound; whether a benefit that is hidden or a benefit that is concealed;
whether a benefit that is guidable or a benefit that is definitive (nīta); or whether a benefit that is blameless, free from defilement, or purified.
Whether it be the conventional meaning or the ultimate meaning, all that revolves within the Buddha’s knowledge.
Every bodily action of the Buddha, the Blessed One, follows after his knowledge; every verbal action follows after his knowledge; every mental action follows after his knowledge.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, possesses unimpeded knowledge regarding the past, unimpeded knowledge regarding the future, and unimpeded knowledge regarding the present. To the extent that there is an object to be known, to that same extent there is knowledge; to the extent that there is knowledge, to that same extent there is an object to be known.
Knowledge has the knowable as its limit, and the knowable has knowledge as its limit. Knowledge does not proceed beyond the knowable, nor is there a path of the knowable beyond knowledge.
These phenomena stand as mutual limits.
Just as when two caskets with lids are perfectly joined, the lower lid does not overstep the upper lid, and the upper lid does not overstep the lower lid, they stand as mutual limits.
In the same way, for the Buddha, the Blessed One, the knowable and knowledge stand as mutual limits.
As far as the knowable extends, so far extends knowledge; as far as knowledge extends, so far extends the knowable. Knowledge has the knowable as its limit; the knowable has knowledge as its limit.
Knowledge does not proceed beyond the knowable, nor is there a path of the knowable beyond knowledge.
Those phenomena exist with one another as their limit.
The knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One, operates regarding all phenomena.
All phenomena are dependent upon the advertence, the desire, the attention, and the arising of consciousness of the Buddha, the Blessed One.
The knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One, extends toward all beings.
And the Blessed One knows the disposition of all beings, he knows their latent tendencies, he knows their conduct, he knows their inclinations;

he knows those with little dust in their eyes and those with much dust in their eyes, those with sharp faculties and those with dull faculties, those of good character and those of bad character, and those who are easy to instruct and those who are difficult to instruct.
He knows beings who are capable and incapable of being instructed.
The world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, revolves within the range of the Buddha’s knowledge.
Just as whatever fish and turtles there are, including even the *timitimiṅgala*, revolve within the great ocean, [so too does this world revolve within the Buddha’s knowledge].
In the same way, the world with its gods, its Māras, and its Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans,
revolves within the range of a Buddha’s knowledge.

Just as whatever birds there may be— even including the Garuḍa, the son of Vinatā— revolve within a portion of space, even so those who are endowed with wisdom equal to that of Sāriputta revolve within a portion of a Buddha’s knowledge.
The Buddha’s knowledge stands having pervaded and surpassed the wisdom of gods and humans.
Even those wise khattiyas, wise brahmins, wise householders, and wise ascetics— subtle thinkers who have mastered the doctrines of others,
who move as if piercing with the barb of a hair, appearing to split apart the positions of views with their own range of wisdom— even they, having formulated questions...
Having prepared their questions, they approach the Tathāgata and ask about things that are hidden and concealed.
Those questions, when answered and resolved by the Blessed One, are explained with their underlying reasons;
and those questions, once cast before the Blessed One, turn out to be successful.
Then indeed the Blessed One outshines everything there—
that is to say, by wisdom.
Thus the Blessed One is possessed of vision through the eye of wisdom as well.
How is the Blessed One possessed of vision even by means of the Buddha-eye?

Surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, the Blessed One saw beings with little dust and much dust, with sharp faculties and dull faculties, of good disposition and bad disposition, easy to instruct and difficult to instruct; and he saw some who dwell perceiving the fear of blame regarding the world beyond.
Just as in a pond of blue lotuses, or pink lotuses, or white lotuses, some blue lotuses, pink lotuses,
or white lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, do not rise above the water,
and thrive submerged within it; while some blue lotuses, pink lotuses, or white lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water...
standing level with the water— some blue lotuses, pink lotuses, or white lotuses,
born in the water, grown in the water, rising up above the water, standing unsullied by the water— even so, the Blessed One,
surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, saw beings with little dust on their eyes and those with much dust on their eyes.

The Blessed One knows: "This person has keen faculties, this one has dull faculties; this one is of good character, this one is of bad character; this one is easy to instruct, this one is difficult to instruct; some dwell seeing the fear of blame and the world beyond. He knows:

"This person is of lustful temperament, this one is of hateful temperament, this one is of deluded temperament, this one is of discursive temperament, this one is of faithful temperament, this one is of intellectual temperament."
For a person of lustful temperament, the Blessed One speaks on the foul;
for a person of hateful temperament, the Blessed One explains the meditation on loving-kindness;

for a person of deluded temperament, the Blessed One establishes them in brief instruction and inquiry, in hearing the Dhamma at the proper time, in discussion of the Dhamma at the proper time, and in living with a teacher.
For a person of discursive temperament, the Blessed One teaches mindfulness of breathing;

for a person of faithful temperament, the Blessed One teaches the sign that inspires confidence: the Buddha’s perfect enlightenment, the Dhamma’s excellence as Dhamma, the Saṅgha’s good practice, and the precepts;
and for a person of a temperament characterized by their own knowledge, the Blessed One teaches the sign for insight: the aspect of impermanence, the aspect of suffering, and the aspect of non-self.
“Just as one standing on the summit of a mountain Might see the people all around,
so too, O wise one, is the Dhamma made of truth.”
Having ascended the palace, O All-Seeing One,
free from sorrow, look down upon the people overwhelmed by grief,
who are overcome by birth and old age.
Thus the Blessed One is possessed of vision by means of the Buddha-eye.
How is the Blessed One possessed of vision by means of the all-around eye?
"All-around eye" refers to omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutañāṇa*).
The Blessed One is endowed with, fully endowed with, has attained, fully attained, is possessed of, fully possessed of,
and is equipped with all-knowing wisdom. "There is nothing here that he has not seen,
nor anything that is unknown or not to be known."
“He has directly known everything that is to be known;
therefore the Tathāgata is one with all-seeing vision.
Thus the Blessed One is an eye-bearer by virtue of his all-seeing vision.
"The One with Vision did not answer me.

O Queen, I have heard that up to three times he does answer; thus, when asked a question consistent with the Dhamma up to three times, the Buddha answers and does not evade it—this is how I have learned it, this is how I have reflected upon it, this is how I have discerned it."
"Devīsī" means both the Blessed One and a seer (isi)— thus, "Devīsī.
Just as kings who have gone forth are called *rājisayo*, and brahmins who have gone forth are called *brāhmaṇisayo*, even so, [he is] both the Blessed One and a seer— thus, "Devīsī."
You are a goddess.
Or else, the Blessed One is an *isi* because he has gone forth;
or he is an *isi* because he sought, searched for, and pursued the great aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*).
The great aggregate of concentration … the great aggregate of wisdom … the great aggregate of liberation …
He is called an *isi* because he sought, searched for, and pursued the great aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
He is called an *isi* because he sought, searched for, and pursued the shattering of the great mass of darkness.
He is called an *isi* because he sought, searched for, and pursued the breaking apart of the great perversion.
The extraction of the great shaft of craving… the untying of the great snare of views… the felling of the great banner of conceit…
The subsiding of great conditioned activity;
the crossing over of the great flood;
the laying down of the great burden.
The cutting off of the great cycle of saṃsāra;
the extinguishing of the great fever;
the allaying of the great burning.
One who raises, seeks, and searches for the great banner of the Dhamma is also called an *isi*.
[One who raises] the great foundations of mindfulness… the great right efforts…
The great faculties… the great powers… the great factors of enlightenment…
He is called an *isi* because he sought, searched for, and pursued the great Noble Eightfold Path;
or because he sought, searched for, and pursued the great ultimate goal, the deathless *nibbāna*;
or because he was sought, searched for, and pursued by beings of great influence.
“Where is the Buddha? Where is the Blessed One? Where is the God of Gods?
Where is the Bull among Men?”—thus I have heard the seer (isi) replied to the queen up to three times.
That is why the brahmin said:
“Twice I questioned Sakka,” said the Venerable Mogharāja,
“but the One with Vision did not answer me.”
"And up to the third time, O Queen,
it was proclaimed— so have I heard:
'This world and the world beyond.'"
Even the Brahma-world together with its devas does not understand the view of the illustrious Gotama.
"This world and the other world.
"This world" refers to the human world.
"The other world" refers to everything other than the human world.
"This world and the other world;
the world with its devas," that is, the world with its devas, its Māras, and its Brahmās, this generation with its recluses and brahmins, its devas and humans—
this is "the world with its devas and Brahmā."

“Diṭṭhiṁ te nābhijānāti” means: the world does not know your view, your preference, your inclination, your conviction, your disposition, or your intention—that is, it does not know, see, perceive, attain, find, or acquire [the knowledge]: “This one has such a view, such a preference, such an inclination, such a conviction, such a disposition, and such an intention.
Thus, “it does not thoroughly know your view.”
"Of Gotama the illustrious": the Blessed One is "illustrious" because he has attained renown.

Alternatively, the Blessed One is "illustrious" because he is honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and respected, and is a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick—thus he is illustrious:
"of Gotama the illustrious."
Therefore that brahmin said:
“This world and the other world,
the Brahmā-world together with its devas;”
“They do not understand the view of the illustrious Gotama.
Thus, [he spoke] of one who has seen what is excellent.
I have come with a question:
How is it that the King of Death does not see one who contemplates the world?

"Thus one of excellent vision": thus one who has excellent vision, supreme vision, best vision, most excellent vision, preeminent vision, highest vision, and ultimate vision—thus "one of excellent vision.
"I have come with a question, seeking the meaning; I have come desiring the meaning... [and so forth].
"This is the burden for you"—thus there is a source for the question.
"How does one look upon the world? means: how does one look upon, review, weigh, judge, discern, and make manifest the world?—this is "how one looks upon the world."
"King Death does not see" means that King Death does not see, does not perceive, does not reach, does not find, and does not obtain— thus,
"King Death does not see.
Therefore, that brahmin said:
“Thus, to one who has such excellent vision,
I have come with a question:
How does one who contemplates the world— ”
The King of Death does not see him.
O Mogharāja, always mindful, look upon the world as empty.
Having uprooted the view of self,
one may thus be a crosser over death;
thus beholding the world, one is a crosser over death.
The King of Death does not see it.
"Behold the world as empty":

here, "the world" refers to the world of hell-beings, the world of animals, the world of hungry ghosts, the world of humans, the world of devas, the world of aggregates, the world of elements, the world of sense-bases; this world, the other world, the Brahma-world, and the world with its devas.
A certain bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
“‘The world, the world,’ it is said, venerable sir.
In what way, venerable sir, is it called ‘the world’?”
“It disintegrates, bhikkhu, therefore it is called ‘the world.
And what disintegrates?
The eye, bhikkhu, disintegrates; forms disintegrate; eye-consciousness disintegrates; eye-contact disintegrates...”
It disintegrates; and whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too disintegrates.
The ear disintegrates...
Odors disintegrate... [and so on] ...the body disintegrates; tangibles disintegrate; the mind disintegrates;

mental phenomena disintegrate; mind-consciousness disintegrates; mind-contact disintegrates; and whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too disintegrates.
“It is because it decays, bhikkhu, that the world is so called.

“One should look upon the world as empty”: one looks upon the world as empty for two reasons—either by way of observing the occurrence of what has been determined, or by way of contemplating formations as hollow.
How does one view the world as empty by way of observing its occurrence as determined?
One finds no mastery over form, no mastery over feeling, no mastery over perception, no mastery over volitional formations, and no mastery over consciousness.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, form is not-self.
For if, bhikkhus, this form were self, then this form would not lead to affliction, and one could exercise mastery over it thus:
‘Let my form be thus; let my form not be thus.’”
But because form, monks, is not-self, therefore form leads to affliction, and it is not possible regarding form [to say]:
"Let my form be thus; let my form not be thus.
Feeling is not-self.
If, monks, this feeling were the self, then this feeling would not lead to affliction, and one could exercise mastery over feeling, saying:
"Let my feeling be thus; let my feeling not be thus.
But because, monks, feeling is not-self, therefore feeling leads to affliction, and one cannot exercise mastery over feeling.
‘May my feeling be thus; may my feeling not be thus.
Perception is non-self.
For if, monks, perception were self, this perception would not lead to affliction, and one could obtain [the wish] regarding perception: [‘May my perception be thus; may my perception not be thus.’]
‘May my perception be thus; may my perception not be thus.
But because perception, monks, is non-self, therefore perception leads to affliction, and it is not possible regarding perception to say:
‘May my perception be thus; may my perception not be thus.’
Formations are non-self.
For if, monks, these formations were self, then these formations would not lead to affliction, and one could exercise mastery over them, saying:
"Let my formations be thus; let my formations not be thus."
But because, monks, volitional formations are non-self, therefore volitional formations lead to affliction; and it is not possible regarding volitional formations:
"Let my volitional formations be thus; let my volitional formations not be thus.
Consciousness is non-self.
If consciousness here, monks, were the self, this consciousness would not lead to affliction, and one could exercise mastery over consciousness, saying:
"Let my consciousness be thus; let my consciousness not be thus.
But because consciousness, monks, is not-self, therefore consciousness leads to affliction, and one cannot exercise mastery over consciousness.
‘May my consciousness be thus; may my consciousness not be thus.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Monks, this body does not belong to you, nor does it belong to others.”
“Monks, this kamma—wrought and intended—is to be regarded as something that must be experienced.
In this regard, monks, the well-taught noble disciple attends closely and thoroughly to dependent origination thus:
‘When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises.’”
When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases. That is to say:

with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise;
with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises; with contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises.
With craving as condition, clinging arises; with clinging as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises;
with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come into being.
Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
"But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations, the cessation of consciousness...
[and so on] ...with the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
In this way, one contemplates the world as empty by means of observing its occurrence as it has been determined.
How does one view the world as empty by way of contemplating formations as hollow?
One finds no core in form, no core in feeling, no core in perception, no core in formations, and no core in consciousness.

Form is coreless, devoid of core, and bereft of core—whether by way of the core of permanence, the core of pleasure, or the core of self; or by way of being permanent, stable, eternal, or subject to non-change.
Feeling is substanceless, devoid of substance, and lacking essence;
perception is substanceless, devoid of substance, and lacking essence;
mental formations are substanceless, devoid of substance, and lacking essence.

Consciousness is without core, coreless, devoid of core—whether by way of the core of permanence, the core of happiness, or the core of self; whether as permanent, stable, eternal, or not subject to change.
Just as a reed is without core, coreless, and devoid of core; and just as a castor-oil plant...
[and so on] ...and just as a fig tree is without core, coreless, and devoid of core; and just as a white thorn-apple tree is without core, coreless, and devoid of core.
Just as a pālibhaddaka horse is without core, devoid of core, and bereft of core; just as a mass of foam is without core, devoid of core, and bereft of core;
just as a bubble on the water is without core, devoid of core, and bereft of core; just as a mirage is without core, devoid of core, and bereft of core;
just as the trunk of a plantain tree is without core, devoid of core, and bereft of core—just so...

Illusion is pithless, substanceless, devoid of essence—in the same way, form is pithless, substanceless, devoid of essence, whether by way of the essence of permanence, the essence of pleasure, or the essence of self; or by way of being permanent, stable, eternal, or not subject to change.
Feeling is pithless, substanceless, devoid of essence … [and so on] … [feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness].
Perception is worthless, pithless, devoid of essence...
mental formations are worthless, pithless, devoid of essence...

consciousness is worthless, pithless, devoid of essence—whether by way of the essence of permanence, the essence of happiness, or the essence of self; or whether it be permanent, stable, eternal, or subject to no change.
Thus, by way of contemplating formations as empty, he contemplates the world as empty.
He contemplates the world as empty for these two reasons.
Furthermore, he contemplates the world as empty in six ways.
The eye is empty of a self or of what belongs to a self, of permanence, of stability, of eternity, or of anything not subject to change;
the ear is empty … the nose is empty … [and so forth].
The tongue is empty ...
the body is empty ...
the mind is empty of a self or of what belongs to a self, of permanence, of stability, of eternity, or of anything not subject to change.
Forms are empty … sounds are empty … odors are empty … [tastes are empty … tangibles are empty … mental phenomena are empty] …pe… thoughts are empty.
Tastes are empty ...
tangibles are empty ...
mental phenomena are empty of a self or of what belongs to a self, of permanence, of stability, of eternity, or of anything that is not subject to change.
Eye-consciousness is empty … mind-consciousness is empty … eye-contact is empty … [and so on] … mental contact is empty.
Mental contact is empty;
feeling born of eye-contact is empty;
feeling born of mind-contact is empty.
Perception of forms is empty … perception of mental phenomena is empty … volition regarding forms is empty …
Volition regarding mental phenomena is empty...
craving for forms is empty...
thought concerning forms is empty...
Investigation of form is empty ...
investigation of mental phenomena is empty of a self or of what belongs to a self, of permanence, of stability, of eternity, or of anything not subject to change.
Thus he contemplates the world as empty in six ways.
Moreover, he contemplates the world as empty in ten aspects:
he contemplates form as void, hollow, empty, non-self, pithless, murderous, subject to dissolution, the root of suffering, subject to taints, and conditioned;
[he contemplates] feeling ... and so on.
perception … volitional formations … consciousness …
passing away … rebirth … re-linking …
He contemplates existence—
and the cycle of saṃsāra— as empty, vain, void, non-self, coreless, murderous, subject to dissolution, the root of suffering, subject to taints, and conditioned.
Thus he surveys the world as empty in ten ways.
Moreover, he contemplates the world as empty in twelve aspects:

form is not a being, not a life-principle, not a person, not a youth, not a woman, not a man, not a self, not belonging to a self, not "I," not "mine," not anyone, and not anything belonging to anyone;
feeling ... [and so on] ... [as above].
Perception...
volitional formations...

consciousness is not a being, not a soul, not a person, not a youth, not a woman, not a man, not a self, not anything belonging to a self; it is not "I," not "mine," nothing at all, and nothing belonging to anyone.
Thus one contemplates the world as empty in twelve ways.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, whatever is not yours, abandon it.”
That which has been abandoned by you will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.
And what, monks, is not yours?
Form, monks, is not yours; abandon it.
That being abandoned will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.
Feeling, monks, is not yours; abandon it.
That being abandoned will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.
"Perception, monks, is not yours; abandon it.
When it is abandoned by you, that will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.
Volitional formations, monks, are not yours; abandon them."
When these have been abandoned by you, they will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.
Consciousness, monks, is not yours; abandon it.
When it has been abandoned by you, it will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.
“Bhikkhus, suppose that whatever grass, wood, branches, and foliage there is in this Jeta’s Grove were to be carried away by people, or burned, or used as they please.
Would it occur to you:
‘People are carrying us away, or burning us, or using us as they please’?”
“No, venerable sir.
“For what reason?
“Because, venerable sir, this is neither our self nor what belongs to our self.”
“In the same way, monks, whatever is not yours, abandon it.
When you have abandoned it, that will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.
And what, monks, is not yours?
“Bhikkhus, form is not yours; abandon it.
When it is abandoned by you, that will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.
Feeling …” [and so on].
Perception, monks, ... volitional formations, ... consciousness is not yours; abandon it.
"That which has been abandoned by you will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.
Thus he contemplates the world as empty.
The Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, it is said: ‘The world is empty, the world is empty.
To what extent, venerable sir, is it said that ‘the world is empty’?
“Because, Ānanda, it is empty of a self or of anything belonging to a self, therefore it is said that ‘the world is empty.’”
And in what way, Ānanda, is it empty of a self or of anything belonging to a self?
The eye, Ānanda, is empty of a self or of anything belonging to a self.
Visible forms are empty … [and so on] …
Eye-consciousness is empty...
eye-contact is empty...
and whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by eye-contact, that too is empty of a self or of anything belonging to a self.
The ear is empty...
sounds are empty...
the nose is empty...
Odors are empty … the tongue is empty … tastes are empty …
The body is empty … tangible objects are empty … the mind is empty …
Phenomena are empty;
mind-consciousness is empty;
mind-contact is empty.
“Whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by mental contact, that too is empty of a self or of what belongs to a self.
And because, Ānanda, it is empty of a self or of what belongs to a self, therefore the world is said to be ‘empty.
In this way, too, he contemplates the world as empty.
“For one who sees, as it truly is, the pure arising of phenomena and the pure continuity of conditioned formations,”
There is no fear, headman, when one sees with wisdom the world as being like grass and sticks.
He desires nothing else whatsoever,
other than for rebirth.
Thus he contemplates the world as empty.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
"In the same way, monks, a monk investigates form as far as the extent of form reaches;
he investigates feeling as far as the extent of feeling reaches."
He investigates perception as far as the range of perception extends;
he investigates volitional formations as far as the range of volitional formations extends;
he investigates consciousness as far as the range of consciousness extends.
As he investigates form, to whatever extent form extends;
[he investigates] feeling … perception … [and so on].

“By scrutinizing volitional formations … consciousness, to the extent that there is a destination for consciousness— even that which he has as ‘I’ or ‘mine’ or ‘I am,’ that too does not exist for him.
In this way, too, he contemplates the world as empty.
"Behold the world as empty": behold the world as empty; review it, see it, weigh it, examine it, discern it, make it manifest—thus, "behold the world as empty.
"Mogharāja, always mindful."
"Mogharāja," the Blessed One addressed that brahmin by name.
"Always" means at all times...
[and so on] ...in the final stage of life.
"He is mindful" by reason of four causes:
when one develops the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the body as a body,
one is mindful … [as before] … thus one is called "mindful."
O Mogharāja, always mindful, uproot the view of self.
"View of self" refers to the twenty-based personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*).
Here, the uninstructed worldling, who has not seen the Noble Ones, is unskilled in the Dhamma of the Noble Ones and undisciplined in the Dhamma of the Noble Ones.
One who does not see true persons, who is unskilled in the Dhamma of true persons, and undisciplined in the Dhamma of true persons,
regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form;
[likewise] feeling … [and so on].

He regards perception as self, or self as possessing perception, or perception as in self, or self as in perception; he regards volitional formations as self... he regards consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness.
Any such view, a resort to views, a thicket of views, a wilderness of views, a distortion of views, a vacillation of views,
a fetter of views, grasping, seizing, adherence, misapprehension, a wrong path, a false course, falsity,
a sectarian standpoint, a perverted grasp, a distorted grasp, a subverted grasp, a wrong grasp, regarding that which is not as it really is.
"According to how it is" refers to the grasping of the sixty-two types of speculative views; this is the view of self (*attānudiṭṭhi*).

"Having uprooted the view of self" means: having uprooted the view of self, having completely uprooted it, having pulled it out, having completely pulled it out, having torn it away, having completely torn it away, having abandoned it, having dispelled it, having brought it to an end, having caused it to cease to exist—this is "having uprooted the view of self."

“Thus one may be a crosser of death”: thus one may cross over death; one may cross over old age; one may cross over death; one may go beyond it, cross over it, transcend it, and pass beyond it—thus one may be a crosser of death.
“Thus observing the world”: thus observing, reviewing, weighing, scrutinizing, discerning, and making clear the world—thus.
When one thus contemplates the world, the King of Death does not see him.
Here, "the King of Death" refers to Māra as the King of Death, Māra the Evil One as the King of Death, and even death itself as the King of Death.
"Does not see" means that the King of Death does not see, does not perceive, does not encounter, does not find, and does not obtain him.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, just as a forest-dwelling deer, while roaming in the forest glade, goes with confidence, stands with confidence, sits with confidence, and lies down with confidence. Why is that?
"He has gone beyond the range of the hunter, monks.

In the same way, monks, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
This, monks, is called a bhikkhu who has blinded Māra, who has struck down Māra’s eye so that it is footless, and has passed beyond the sight of the Evil One."

Furthermore, monks, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, a monk enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal tranquility and unification of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of concentration;
... [and so on] ... he enters and dwells in the third jhāna; ... he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
“Monks, this is called a monk who has blinded Māra; having struck down Māra’s eye, he has passed beyond the sight of the Evil One.

Furthermore, monks, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking ‘space is infinite,’ a monk enters and dwells in the base of infinite space.
This, monks, is called a monk who has blinded Māra; having struck down Māra’s eye, he has passed beyond the sight of the Evil One.”
Furthermore, monks, by completely transcending the base of infinite space, [perceiving] "consciousness is infinite," a monk enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness… Furthermore,
monks, by completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, [perceiving] "there is nothing," a monk enters and dwells in the base of nothingness… Furthermore,
monks, by completely transcending the base of nothingness, a monk enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception…
Furthermore, monks, by completely transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling;
and having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed.
This, monks, is called a monk who has blinded Māra, who, having struck down Māra’s eye so that it is footless, has gone beyond the sight of the Evil One, and has crossed over attachment to the world.
Thus he goes with confidence, stands with confidence, sits with confidence, and lies down with confidence.
Why is that? Because the bhikkhu has come out of the range of the Evil One.”
The King of Death does not see him.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Behold the world as empty."
O Mogharāja, always mindful,
having uprooted the view of a self,
you may thus be one who has crossed over death.
“The King of Death does not see one who thus contemplates the world.
At the conclusion of this verse, …pe… [the earth shook].
"The Blessed One is my Teacher, venerable sir; I am his disciple.
This concludes the fifteenth exposition: the Questions of the Young Brahmin Mogharāja.
